summary:
Mission Architect is an interactive web game where players design, launch, and manage a complete space mission. Players choose a mission (Earth orbit, Moon, asteroid, or Mars), a launch vehicle, propellant, science instruments, passengers, and food fridges. Every decision has a consequence: instruments add science but also mass, power use, data, and cost, and every person on board needs food, so more people means more fridges, which cost mass, power, money, and cabin room. A launch check blocks designs that are too heavy, lack enough delta-v, or do not fit.

After launch, a live simulation shows the battery, data storage, and communications, including the delay before telemetry reaches Earth. Poor power planning can put the spacecraft into safe mode. The game ends with a score and a report that explains why the mission succeeded or failed.

It addresses the challenge by showing how mass, power, budget, data, and communications work together as one system, so students learn real mission-design trade-offs by experimenting. It supports solo play and two-player co-op, in English and French. Values are simplified for education.
Source code: https://github.com/Abdallah-Alfakhouri/KPG-Nova-Nasa
details:
What it does: Mission Architect is a web game where players design a complete space mission. They choose a destination (Earth orbit, Moon, asteroid, or Mars), a launch vehicle, propellant, science instruments, passengers, and food fridges. A launch check blocks designs that are too heavy, do not have enough delta-v, do not fit in the vehicle, or cannot feed the crew. If the launch is approved, a live simulation shows the rocket in flight, with battery, data storage, and communications, including the delay before telemetry reaches Earth. The game ends with a score and a report explaining why the mission succeeded or failed.

Benefits and impact: Students rarely get to see mass, power, budget, data, and communications interact as one system. In our game every choice has a visible cost: more instruments mean more science but also more power and data, and more people mean more food, more fridges, and less room. The aim is to teach trade-offs, not just right and wrong answers.

Creativity: a food and crew system tied to journey length, a rocket animation with a live telemetry link to Earth, two-player co-op, and a profile page featuring real NASA scientists as mentors.

What we considered: educational clarity, realistic constraints (with simplified numbers), solo and two-player play, and replayability.

Tools: The project was built with AI assistance. The initial app was generated in Figma (Figma Make), and later features were added and refined with Claude (Anthropic). The code is React, TypeScript, Vite, and CSS, reviewed and run in VS Code, and hosted on Netlify. Team KPG Nova, ZU University, Jordan directed the design, game rules, and testing.
